item.title: Global IR
item.description:
Acharya’s article read for and discussed in Lecture 4 contains 3 directions IR could move to be more globally representative.The first option is to take what exists of Western International Relations theory today and build on top of it. By adding non-Western cases to existing theories, and perhaps adapting them to be more accurate in all cases, you can build a more inclusive IR field. But this solution still places non-western theory as an addition, an extra layer of testing, rather than including it as a core and equally important part of the research.Developing new theories from Asian experiences, histories, concepts, and practice. This would bring new theories to light but would fail to make IR diverse and representative as you would simply be replacing a Western emphasis with an Asian one, leaving out many cases as subjects of study.Acharya prefers a more balanced approach in which scholars draw on various traditions without preference for any particular region or case. In doing so you expand the scope of IR with an underlying cultural shift amongst academics for what regards adequate scholarship that offers a well rounded image of International Relations that is based in fact, not region.The goal of a global IR would not be to entirely forget western theory but rather to expand it's foundations and mechanisms. It recognizes the Westphalian system as one of many historical traditions of statehood rather than the default. Alternative systems from around the world should be folded in as equal partners, not newly dominant ideas.
Lecture 4

item.title: Non-Western IR Theories
item.description: I fully recognize the irony in the fact that I am constantly comparing and contrasting the descriptions of non-western systems and theories to western IR. But given that is what the rest of the course covers I am using it as a benchmark that I assume most of us to understand. Western IR theory operates on a Westphalian idea of states, the system which arose in Europe following the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. But this is not the only system present. In alternative systems like those that were found in China there typically formed systems of hierarchy rather than pure anarchy as is the view of the Westphalian state system. In Southeast Asia the Mandala system allowed for overlapping authority without the rigid borders that were so fundamental in Europe. Non-western actors are often used only as data points for testing Western theories. In many cases there is little consideration made for these states' decision making, ideas, history, culture, and other particularities. Non-western conceptions of international order are ignored or treated as deviations and outliers in most western literatures.The development of non-western IR has been slow primarily due to structural barriers and reluctance to broaden scope. The slides break them down as follows: Institutional Major journals, publishers, and conferences are often based in the west and by extension have a bias towards locally developed and locally applicable theory. Policy Pull Non-western scholars often pursue the implementation of policies rather than simply forming theories for the sake of having theories. Language English is the dominant language of academia and is most natively spoken in western countries. Area Studies vs IR Non-Western regions are often categorized as "area studies" rather than bing folded into the study of international relations Hegemonic acceptance The dominance of western theory in the culture of academia and international politics can lead non-western scholars to internalize assumptions the western theory is better and what should be pursued. Lecture 4

item.title: Imagined Communities
item.description: Benedict Anderson proposed the concept of imagined communities in his book of the same name. He made the declaration that nations are imagined communities. His argument centered around the idea that nations, and national identity, are socially constructed phenomena. Anderson emphasizes how nations generate a sense of community where you do not and will never know every individual in the nation, this is where the imagined aspect comes from. Nations are not natural or pre-existing entities but constructions characterized by their; Limitedness Even the largest nation have finite boundaries which define who is and who is not a part of the nation. This othering contributes to peoples sense of belonging and identity. Sovereignty The idea of the nation arose at the same time as the movement for self government largely along national lines Community Despite internal inequalities and differences, members of a nation imagine themselves as part of a deep, horizontal comradeship, sharing a common identity and purpose. This imagined fraternity fosters solidarity and can motivate individuals to make sacrifices for the nation.

item.title: The Security Dilemma
item.description: The security dilemma is the endless cycle of pursuing securitization. This occurs because when one state desires the most security they can obtain, other states become less secure relative to that state. The consequently want to become more secure to compensate, making states who don't securitize even less secure, and so on and so forth. It can be represented a little better visually.The following dynamics contribute to this dilemma: Defensive measures of other states are perceived as offensive threats towards your own state Uncertainty about other states' intentions since they have no obligation to be honest in an anarchic system States may enter an arms race despite neither state intending to fight an offensive war Example: Nuclear Weapons Following the development of the atom bomb by the United States and the subsequence uses against Japan, other states, notably the Soviet Union, also pursued the bomb. Seeing other states obtain the bomb, the United States built more, in turn so did the Soviet Union.

item.title: Nuclear Security
item.description:
Since 1945 nuclear proliferation has been a major concern in global security. Warhead counts reached their highest numbers in the late 1980s and have been steadily decreasing since. But the threat remains looming. International Relations has developed the following concepts for discussing nuclear security.Nuclear deterrence is the phenomena in which the possibility of a retaliatory nuclear strike prevents an attack from occurring. Example The United States posses nuclear weapons, this makes it less likely that Russia will launch their nuclear weapons due to the high likelihood the United States would immediately strike back with their own nukes. Extended deterrence is a connected idea that states with nukes can open a "nuclear umbrella" which theoretically commits to protecting other states using your nukes in the event of a nuclear strike on them.Example Russia strikes the Netherlands with nukes. In response the United States nukes Russia on the Netherlands' behalf. Underlying the deterrence mentioned above is the concept of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD). The MAD doctrine states that the use of nuclear weapons against another nuclear power (or a state under their nuclear umbrella) only ensures that both states will be destroyed in nuclear war.First strike capability is rather straightforward, referring to the ability to launch a nuclear strike. Any states with nuclear warheads and the means by which to deliver them to a target has first strike capability. Second strike capability refers to the ability to be struck and retaliate following the detonation of nuclear weapon(s) in your territory.The nuclear taboo is the propensity for states and their representatives not to use nuclear weapons, and in many instances extends to not threatening the use of nuclear weapons.Nuclear proliferation refers to the spread of and stockpiling of nuclear weapons. The Sagan reading "Why Do States Build Nuclear Weapons?" offers 3 models of nuclear proliferation which were also reviewed in the lecture
The security model proposes that states build nuclear weapons in pursuit of national security against external threats. This is linked to Neorealist thinking. The core logic is that states react to external threats (such as other states possessing nukes) by constructing their own weapons and by extension benefiting from Nuclear Deterrence. A historical example of this is the Soviet Union. Following Hiroshima Stalin reportedly told Soviet scientists:Joseph Stalin "Provide us with atomic weapons in the shortest possible time. You know that Hiroshima has shaken the whole world. The balance has been destroyed. provide the bomb - it will remove a great danger from us." The domestic politics model proposes that states build nuclear weapons as political tools leveraged by domestic actors like the military, bureaucrats, and politicians to advance their own interest. It identifies 3 classes of actors who can benefit: The Nuclear Energy Establishment Nuclear scientists and nuclear laboratories seeking funding and prestige are likely to play a role in promoting atomic weapon development The Military Military services and units who would be allocated additional resources and missions from a nuclear arsenal are likely to play a role as well Politicians Politicians involved in the development of nuclear weapons are likely to use this to their political advantage. The norms model proposes that states build nuclear weapons as signs of national prestige, modernity, and status. The bomb is a symbol of technological achievement and comes with a certain role on the world stage. States who desire that position may pursue it for that reason.

item.title: Two Faces of Nationalism
item.description: International Relations identifies two manifestations of Nationalism, sometimes called the civic-ethnic axis. These two faces of nationalism are not mutually exclusive and can be found at the same time to varying degrees of intensity. All instances of nationalism have a mix of each of the following versions, the study of nationalism therefore becomes identifying which one is stronger in a given case.Civic nationalism is an attachment to the nation in an institutional sense. You feel connected to its institutions, laws, and commitments. Civic nationalism is relatively inclusive, theoretically it means anyone participating and adhering to the structures and values of the nation is a part of the nation.Ethnic nationalism is an attachment to the nation in an ancestral sense. You feel connected to the language, religion, shared history, and genetics of the nation. Membership is more rigid and is considered inherit to the individual from birth due to their parents' own connection to the nation.

item.title: Liberal International Order
item.description: The idea of the Liberal International Order is a theory within the tradition of Liberalism. The theory aims to explain how power and institutions combine to sustain order as was the case with the post-war American led system. As a part of the liberal school it builds on concepts like neoliberal institutionalism, republican liberalism, and interdependence liberalism. It uses these to explain why leading states choose to accept the rules and constraints of the international order. The order depends on a sense of legitimacy, as well as restraint from dominant states.

item.title: Rodrik's Globalization Trilemma
item.description:
The Globalization Trilemma was put simply by Rodrik:Rodrik (2011) pg. 200 "We cannot simultaneously pursue democracy, national self-determination, and economic globalization" His argument is that you can not have substantive amounts of all 3 pursuits at once. To have the nation-state as well as globalization, you must sacrifice democracy. To have globalization as well as democracy, you must sacrifice the nation-state. And finally to have democracy and nation-states, you must sacrifice deep globalization. The following images from the slides display this well.Trilemma visualized
The Trilemma in a Table In the lecture Denney goes more in depth on each of these so if it doesn't click for you in a blob of text, try the web lecture it was worth it for me. During the Eurozone crisis Greece adopted austerity policies imposed by Troika (EC, ECB, IMF). In 2015 the Greek people voted on agreement terms and voted 61% against. The Greek government later accepted even harsher terms than the ones on the ballot. In this case Greece maintained its pursuit of globalization and the sovereignty of the nation-state. They sacrificed democracy by overriding the population's vote on the issue.The United Kingdom voted 51.9% in favor of leaving the European Union in 2016. The officially left in 2020. In this case the UK maintained sovereignty and democracy at the expense of globalization. Sovereignty by way of returning to full policy control, democracy was maintained by adhering to the referendum results, globalization was lost by leaving the single market and re-raising barriers to trade and (geo)political cooperation.

item.title: Constructivism
item.description:
Constructivism, alongside Realism and Liberalism, is one of the 3 "traditional IR theories". Fundamentally, it believes states behave rationally within a anarchic system.Constructivism traditionally believes that states act not only on power in a material sense, but also based on shared values, ideas, and identities. State interest is shaped by identity, identity is shaped by historical, social, and political contexts which are sometimes shared between states. The common norms and values within a state manifest themselves in the acts of the state. It differs from realism and liberalism, which both take state interests as a given. But constructivism asks how these interests are formed and what influences them.Wendt, 1992 "Anarchy is what states make of it" Constructivism disagrees with both realism and liberalism. Anarchy guarantees neither conflict nor cooperation. Instead, anarchy leaves the power in the hands of states to guide how they interact.
Lecture 2 slides 14-16

item.title: Liberalism
item.description:
Liberalism, alongside Realism and Constructivism, is one of the 3 "traditional IR theories". Fundamentally, it believes states behave rationally within a anarchic system.
Liberalism traditionally believes that conflict is not an inevitable consequence of the international system. Liberalism agrees with realism that the international system exists in anarchy. But liberalism differs in their belief that through mutually agreed upon rules, laws, organizations, and norms conflict can be avoided. Like Neoclassical realism, liberalism believes that the domestic politics of a state influence that states foreign policy. Ultimately liberalism recognizes that the institutions and norms have not yet prevented conflict entirely, but liberalism is underlined by the belief that international politics can become more stable and cooperative with the appropriate steps. Interdependence liberalism argues that economic exchange makes states dependent on one another. This consequently would make a conflict with that other state more expensive and disruptive. Thus the belief is that a rational state would be less likely to engage in that conflict, and would seek an alternative solution to resolve whatever issue there may be. A key example of this turned into a policy is the European Union and its predecessors.Republican liberalism argues that i a democratic system, domestic institutions constrain leaders. This argument is centered around the idea that leaders who hold power at the will of the electorate, will not want to fight a war which makes them unpopular, and therefore less likely to reelected. The idea for international relations is therefore that democratic countries will find alternative mechanisms through which to resolve disputes. Neoliberal institutionalism argues that global institutions facilitate cooperation even inside of an anarchic systems. For this theory, institutions can correct for the uncertainty that is a key assumption of realism. With reduced uncertainty states act with more trust for one another because the institutions provide a certain guarantee that other states will behave "appropriately".
Lecture 2 slides 10-13

item.title: Realism
item.description:
Realism, alongside Liberalism and Constructivism, is one of the 3 "traditional IR theories". Fundamentally, it is concerned with power; which states have it, which do not, and how that influences state relations.Realism traditionally assumes that global politics is at its heart about power struggles between states. It believes this to be the case because for realists, the international system is one of anarchy. They argue that anarchy is the reality of the international system because there is no higher authority than the state. Consequently, states are said to first and foremost value survival and security as well as the pursuit of greater power. This is also called Power Politics. Though it is important to note that there is variation amongst realists and not all realist theories are the same.Classical realism sees power politics as a consequence of human nature. Classical realists argue that there is egoistic and selfish tendency to human nature which then manifests itself in state behavior. Morgenthau, 1962 "The social world is but a projection of human nature onto the collective plane" Neorealism, also called structural realism, argues that state behavior is first and foremost influenced by the (anarchic) structure of the international system. Unlike classical realism, human nature is not the cause of conflict. Instead they argue the anarchy of the international system is what causes competition. There are varying perspectives on how states react to structural pressures. Uncertainty The uncertainty described in neorealism comes from the fact that, in anarchy, there is no way to know for certain that another state is being honest. They may tell you they want to be friendly and maintain good relations, whilst at the same time mobilizing to invade you. This is then said to lead states to assume the worst, making them pursue power as a matter of security and self preservation in the event of conflict. The fundamental assumption of offensive neorealism is that, in an anarchic system, it is uncertainty of other states' intentions that push states to pursue more power for themselves. As such great powers pursue the greatest relative power possible. Offensive realists argue that great powers can only truly achieve regional hegemony as the greatest extent of their power.Defensive realism conceptualizes states as pursuing security, not power. The argument is that excessive power accumulation makes other states perceive you as a threat. If you expand too much (territorially or otherwise) other states will seek to counter-balance this strength which would have the consequence of reducing security. Instead of pursuing power for power's sake, states pursue security by utilizing "balancing strategies". There is internal balancing, which builds capabilities: arms manufacturing, infrastructure development suited for military use, or more direct security facilities like fortifications and air defenses). There is external balancing in the form of building alliances with other states. Finally states practice restraint which keeps them from being subject to counter-balancing.Neoclassical realism agrees with neorealism that anarchy matters, but they add another force: domestic factors. Domestic factors may include metrics like a state's capacity to act, the domestic politics and ruling ideology, leadership perceptions and decision-making. For neoclassical realists the dynamic works so that structural pressures provide boundaries on decision making whilst domestic factors shape the ultimate choice of the state.Example: Nazi Germany The Nazis did not expand due only to systemic pressure, but also due to the domestic ideology of the regime.
Lecture 2 slides 4-9
